title: How planes are built
examples: What part of the plane helps it steer?
How do engineers make wings strong enough for flight?
Can you explain what the engines do for the plane?

explain.say: Today we are learning how engineers build airplanes.
First we look at the wings. Wings are shaped to push air down.
Next are the engines. Engines use fuel to create a strong push called thrust.
Then we study control surfaces. These parts help the pilot steer the plane.
Finally, planes need strong materials. Engineers often use aluminum and carbon fibre.
Think about riding a bicycle down a hill. The wheels are like the wings creating lift.

faq.q: Do the wings make the plane fly all by themselves?
faq.a: No, the wings create lift, but the engines provide the forward push, or thrust. This combination keeps the plane moving through the air.
asks: Is lift enough to fly an airplane?

faq.q: What is the difference between the rudder and the ailerons?
faq.a: The rudder controls side-to-side movement, which is called yaw. Ailerons control the bank or roll of the wings.
asks: How do I steer left or right?

faq.q: Why do planes use carbon fibre instead of just metal?
faq.a: Carbon fibre is very strong but also much lighter than many metals. This lightness helps the plane use less fuel.
asks: Why is carbon fibre good for planes?
What material is best for airplanes?

faq.q: Do the engines only push the plane forward?
faq.a: Engines create thrust, which is the force pushing the plane forward. This force must overcome air resistance for steady flight.

faq.q: How do the control surfaces work together?
faq.a: The pilot uses all surfaces together. For example, turning requires adjusting the rudder and ailerons at the same time.
asks: Do all the controls work together?

facts: Lift is the upward force generated by the wings moving through the air.
Thrust is the forward-pushing force provided by the engines.
Control surfaces like the rudder help steer the plane in the air.
Engine materials must be strong enough to handle high heat and pressure.

quiz.say: If the engines suddenly stopped working, what force would immediately become the most critical for keeping the plane stable?
quiz.why: The control surfaces help the pilot manage the plane's attitude even without engine power.

wrong.1: Lift is generated by the wings moving through air, but control surfaces manage the direction.
wrong.2: Thrust is the force from the engines; if they stop, thrust is zero.
wrong.3: Weight is the downward pull of gravity; it is always present.

quiz.say: Which component is primarily responsible for controlling the plane's roll or banking?
quiz.why: Ailerons are on the wings and move up and down to change the lift on each wing slightly.

wrong.0: The rudder controls side movement, which is called yaw.
wrong.1: The elevator controls up and down movement, which is called pitch.
wrong.2: Flaps are usually used to increase lift at slower speeds, not for general rolling.

quiz.say: If an engineer wants to make a plane lighter without losing strength, which material property is most important to consider?
quiz.why: This ratio means the material is very strong compared to how light it is, like carbon fibre.

wrong.0: This relates to surfaces sliding against each other, not the material's inherent strength.
wrong.2: This relates to heat transfer, which is not the main concern for structural weight.
wrong.3: This relates to electricity, not the main structural requirement.
